## Today

- Values of the Founding
- Spectrum of limits on government force
- Discussion: where do *you* place the hard cases?

# Why This Matters

## Why This Matters

::: {.custom-style style="font-size: 55px;"}
By the end of today you will place the Founding on a spectrum of answers to how much we should limit government — and state two modern classical-liberal restatements.
:::

## Bridge

- Government = organized coercive force accepted as legitimate
- Ethics of when force is acceptable
- Founding values: how to live together peacefully as dignified equals

## Two basic questions

1. What is the proper purpose of government?
2. How do we limit government to only those purposes?

# Classical Liberalism

## Classical liberalism

- Limit the power of government
- Expand political participation
- Allow individuals and voluntary associations to flourish

## Modern restatement — Coyne

Live together peacefully in a society of dignified equals.

(close paraphrase of Chris Coyne)

## Legitimate goals of government

Life. Liberty. Pursuit of happiness. Property as the product of labor.

# Spectrum of Limits

## Most restrained

“That government is best which governs not at all.” — Thoreau, *Civil Disobedience* (1849)

## Moderate restraint

“That government is best which governs least.” — *United States Magazine and Democratic Review*

## Krauthammer

The mark of a civilized society is to maintain organized violence at the lowest possible level. — Charles Krauthammer, *Things That Matter* (2013)

## Constitutional limits

Force only when and how a constitution allows.

## The bargain

| The people agree to | The government agrees to |
|---------------------|--------------------------|
| Give up some freedom | Protect fundamental rights |
| Submit to some coercion | Life, liberty, property |

Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau describe different bargains.

# Hard Cases

## Militant democracy and realpolitik

Where do they sit on the spectrum — closer to freedom, or closer to theocracy and totalitarianism?

## Theocracy

Power justified by divine mandate.

## Totalitarianism

“All within the state, nothing against the state, nothing outside the state.” — Mussolini

# Teaser

If you never signed the contract, are you bound by its terms? Later lectures return to that question.
